q: Which task is the best first candidate to delegate to a coding agent?
o: Add unit tests for a well-specified utility module that already has CI
e: It is well-scoped, automatically verifiable and easy to undo via a PR.

q: Agent PRs pass CI but repeatedly miss what the requester wanted. Which gap is most likely?
o: Tasks lack explicit acceptance criteria and scope
e: Without objective success criteria the agent optimizes for 'looks done'.

q: Which setup is an autonomy anti-pattern?
o: Agent pushes to its own branch and opens a draft PR
Agent can merge its own PR to the default branch with no required review
Agent uses a read-only tool list while planning
Agent output is linked to a session log
e: Self-approval removes the independent human control that makes autonomy safe.

q: Select TWO inputs that belong in a well-formed agent task.
o: The entire chat history of unrelated projects
e: Criteria and scope bound the work; broad credentials or unrelated history add risk and noise.

q: Requirement: the agent must propose a change plan and must not modify code until a human approves. Best design?
o: One agent with write tools and an instruction saying 'ask first'
A planner limited to read/search tools that outputs a structured plan, plus an executor enabled only after approval
Let the agent run, then revert if the plan was wrong
e: Tool restriction plus an approval gate technically enforces plan-before-act.

q: Why should an agent emit a structured plan (for example a numbered checklist) rather than free prose?
o: It can be validated and compared with the final diff
e: Structure makes automated and human validation and later comparison possible.

q: Which artifact best supports inspection in standard development tooling?
o: A private chat transcript on a laptop
A draft PR with description, commits and a link to the session log
A screenshot in a slide deck
e: PRs, commits and logs live in tools reviewers already use and are auditable.

q: How can you keep humans in control without slowing delivery?
o: Review at the PR boundary and use CODEOWNERS/rulesets for sensitive paths
e: Risk-based review points keep control with minimal friction.

q: Put a plan-gated agent workflow in order.
o: Agent executes the approved plan and opens a draft PR
Task is defined with acceptance criteria
Automated scans and human review of the PR
Agent produces a structured plan using read-only tools
e: Define, plan (read-only), validate/approve, execute, then scan and review.

q: An agent's plan references a test file that does not exist. Which control would catch this before execution?
e: Validating the plan against the repo catches hallucinated references.

q: Which characteristic most makes a task unsuitable for autonomous delegation?
o: It touches more than one file
Requirements are ambiguous and there is no automated way to verify the result
It is documented in an issue
e: No verification and unclear intent mean the agent cannot know when it is done.

q: An auditor wants to know how an agent change was produced. Which built-in cloud agent evidence helps most?
o: Session logs linked from the agent's commit messages
e: Agent commits link to session logs; commits also record the requester as co-author.

q: Which file gives Copilot persistent, repo-wide guidance such as build commands and conventions?
How should you decide the degree of autonomy for a dependency-bump agent?
o: Classify by risk and apply proportional guardrails, for example PR creation allowed and review required
Let the agent decide for itself
e: Autonomy is right-sized to risk with guardrails.

q: One mega-agent plans, codes, security-reviews and deploys. What is the primary problem?
o: No separation of duties, so no independent check
e: Roles should be separated so reviewing is independent of building.

q: Which is the best definition of done for a bug-fix task?
o: Failing regression test added and passing, suite green, no new CodeQL alerts, changes limited to the affected module
e: Objective, checkable criteria beat self-reported completion.
